text:
Productions
Pixcom inc. c. Fabrikant

2005 QCCA 703

COURT OF
APPEAL

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

REGISTRY OF

MONTRÉAL

No:

500-09-015321-052

DATE:

AUGUST 8, 2005

CORAM:

THE HONOURABLE

PIERRE J. DALPHOND,
J.A.

MARIE-FRANCE BICH,
J.A.

JACQUES DUFRESNE, J.A.

PRODUCTIONS PIXCOM INC

And

LES CHAÎNES TÉLÉ ASTRAL.

PETITIONERS

v.

VALERY
I FABRIKANT

APPELLANT - Petitioner

JUDGMENT

[
1
]

THE COURT
; -
ruling on two motions filed by the Petitioners to dismiss the appeal of the
Respondent from a decision of the Superior Court, District of Montreal (the
Honourable Chief Justice Rolland) rendered on January 5, 2005;

[
2
]

After having examined the file, heard the
parties and deliberated;

[
3
]

For the reasons of Dalphond, J.A., with which
Bich and Dufresne, JJ.A. agree;

[
4
]

GRANTS
the
motions to dismiss the appeal, with costs;

[
5
]

DISMISSES
the
appeal, with costs.

PIERRE J. DALPHOND, J.A.

MARIE-FRANCE
BICH, J.A.

JACQUES
DUFRESNE, J.A.

Mtre Alain-Claude Desforges

Bélanger Sauvé

For the petitioner Pixcom

Mtre Véronique Dubois

Heenan Blaikie srl

For the petitioner Astral

Valery I. Fabrikant

In person (by phone)

Date of hearing:

June 13, 2005

REASONS OF DALPHOND, J.A.

[
6
]

Valery Fabrikant has inscribed in appeal from a
decision conveyed to him by a letter from Chief Justice Rolland of the Quebec
Superior Court, dated January 5, 2005, refusing him authorization to file a
statement of claim against Les chaînes télé Astral, a division of Astral Inc.
(Astral) and Productions Pixcom Inc. (Pixcom).  By motions pursuant to
article
501

C.C.P
., Astral and Pixcom seek the dismissal of the appeal.

[
7
]

This proceeding raises interesting legal issues:
(1) what is the legal status of the reply letter?  (2) if it is to be
considered as a judgment, can Mr. Fabrikant appeal it without leave?  (3)
do Astral and Pixcom have the necessary status to present a motion for the
summary dismissal of Mr. Fabrikant’s appeal?

CONTEXTUAL BACKGROUND

[
8
]

On August 24, 1992, Mr. Fabrikant shot and
killed four of his colleagues at Concordia University and attempted to kill a
fifth.  At the outcome of a long and difficult trial where he continually
attacked the judicial system and the presiding judge as being corrupt, lawless and
criminal, he was found guilty of four counts of first-degree murder, one count
of attempted murder and two counts of illegal confinement.  When pronouncing
the obligatory sentence of life imprisonment in
R
. v.
Fabrikant
,

[1993] Q.J. No. 1443 (S.C.)
, Martin, J. described him as “a warped, twisted and
deeply troubled man”.

[
9
]

In the late 1990’s and at the beginning of the
year 2000, Mr. Fabrikant filed numerous proceedings against a doctor
looking after him while he was detained at the Cowansville penitentiary,
Dr. Corbin, in order to be provided certain specific medical treatments.
He did likewise in the Federal Court
[1]
against the
Canadian Correctional System.

[
10
]

Tired of being exposed to what he considered to
be abusive and frivolous proceedings, Dr. Corbin petitioned the Superior
Court in order to have Mr. Fabrikant declared to be a vexatious litigant.
Following an order of Rolland, J., as he was then, dated May 30,
2000, J.E.
2000-1347 (S.C.)
, Mr. Fabrikant cannot institute any judicial proceedings
before the Quebec Superior Court except with leave of the Chief Justice or a
judge designated by him/her (prohibition order).  Rolland, J. wrote :

[…]

Après avoir entendu Fabrikant, le
tribunal conclut que sans contrôle ou balises, ce dernier ne fera que multiplier
les demandes ou requêtes inutiles, vexatoires, démontrant un mépris total pour
l’administration de la justice, les juges, avocats et ses autres auxiliaires.
D’ailleurs, Fabrikant de sang-froid, affirme au soussigné dans la cause pour
les soins que le jugement à rendre démontrera s’il avait raison de se faire
justice à lui même en référant explicitement aux quatre meurtres qu’il a commis
en 1992 plutôt que d’avoir recours aux tribunaux qu’il dit corrompus.

Rares sont les personnes qui font
preuve d’un tel mépris et abusent des ressources disponibles tant judiciaires
que médicales.

Dans les circonstances, se fondant sur
les
articles 2
,
20
et
46
du
Code de procédure civile du Québec
, le
tribunal déclare Fabrikant, plaideur vexatoire et en conséquence, émet des
ordonnances pour limiter et déterminer les paramètres dans le cadre desquels,
Fabrikant pourra avoir accès aux tribunaux.

[…]

ORDONNE
au
demandeur Valery I. Fabrikant de ne pas directement ou indirectement déposer
devant la Cour Supérieure quelque procédure judiciaire que ce soit,
introductive d’instance, incidente ou interlocutoire sans avoir obtenu
l’autorisation préalable écrite de la juge en chef de la Cour Supérieure ou
d’un juge désigné par elle.

ORDONNE

aux greffiers et autres officiers de justice de la Cour Supérieure de la
province de Québec de ne plus délivrer, timbrer ou enregistrer au plumitif ou
placer sur un rôle de la Cour Supérieure de la province de Québec, toute
procédure intentée par Valery I. Fabrikant à moins qu’une autorisation préalable,
écrite de la juge en chef de la Cour Supérieure ou de tout autre juge désigné
par elle n’apparaisse sur cette procédure.

[
11
]

Mr. Fabrikant appealed the order of
Rolland, J.  His appeal was summarily dismissed by this Court on January 8,
2001 (file 500-09-010076-008).

[
12
]

In the present matter, in November of 2004,
Mr. Fabrikant sought authorization form Rolland, C.J. to file an action in
damages against Astral and Pixcom.  The sole document produced was a brief
draft statement of claim which reads as follows:

Plaintiff respectfully submits:

1.

Defendant Canal D has presented a show about me
at the end of October 2004.  The show is made by Defendant Pixcom and is full
of lies and deliberate distortions.  The purpose of show was libellous: the
present me as a totally insane person, who killed 4 innocent people, who not
only did nothing wrong to him, but rather tried to help him.  Nothing could be
further from the truth.

2.

Defendant Pixcom failed to adhere to the
fundamental principles of professional journalism, and in particular,

a)

Despite my repeated offers to tell my side of
the story, Pixcom refused to interview me;

b)

Pixcom presented a psychiatrist, who declared me
paranoiac, while knowing full well, that this psychiatrist has never met me in
person;

c)

Pixcom failed to inform viewers, that I have
never had any psychiatric problems.  Never visited any psychiatrist, was never
prescribed any anti-psychotic medications and never needed them;

d)

Pixcom failed to check veracity of stories told,
and in particular.  Sheinin’s lies about the content of my phone call to her
and her false claim of my ability to stare at someone without blinking: nobody
can do that.  All was designed to present me as an insane person.

3.

Defendant Pixcom was given full access to all
documents on my web site, so it can not claim honest lack of knowledge.

4.

The purpose of Defendant Pixcom was malicious:
by representing me as an insane person, they managed to hide the truth: big
scoundrels, like former Chief Justice Gold, former Rector Kenniff, Former Vice-Rector
Sheinin et al. had used small scoundrels to threaten my life and thus to
provoke me into shooting.

5.

Defendant Canal D knew or should have known,
that the show it presented was one-sided, deliberately false, designed to hide
the thruth.  Just one fact: at the beginning of the show, the viewer is told
that I did my graduate studies under the top Soviet engineer and then, later
on, the viewer is told that I was unmasked as an impostor, who never had an
engineering degree, but rather a degree in Mathematics.  I studied under a top
engineer and got a degree in Mathematics?  It makes no sense, but Pixcom needed
this nonsense to present this “unmasking” as one of the main reasons for
shooting.

THEREFORE, may it please to court
to:

A)

DECLARE Defendants Pixcom and Canal D jointly
responsible for malicious libel;

B)

ORDER Defendant Pixcom to pay damages to the
Plaintiff in the amount of $ 800,000;

C)

ORDER Defendant Canal D to pay damages to the
Plaintiff in the amount of $ 100,000.

The
whole with costs. (Transcribed as written)

[
13
]

In his letter dated January 5, 2005, Rolland,
C.J. dismissed the request as follows:

[…]

I also acknowledge receipt of your
“Statement of claim” dated November 17, 2004 which, I presume, is in
relation to your letter of November 3, 2004.

Based on the facts alleged in your
Statement of claim, I am of the opinion that your claim is unfounded in law and
your request for authorization is therefore denied.

Please be advised that any future
procedures that you wish to present should be sent to my attention
by mail

accompanied by a formal letter requesting authorization, or it will be returned
to you without notice.

Your procedures
should also
never
be sent to the opposite parties until such time as I have authorized
them.

[
14
]

On January 19, 2005, Mr. Fabrikant filed an
inscription in appeal.

[
15
]

At the request of Robert, C.J.Q. a copy of this
inscription in appeal was served on Astral and Pixcom, which then became aware
of the claim that Mr. Fabrikant wished to file against them.  They each
responded by filing a motion to dismiss summarily the appeal pursuant to
art.
501

C.C.P
. and to declare Mr. Fabrikant a vexatious litigant in
this Court.
[2]

RELEVANT STATUTORY PROVISIONS

[
16
]

COURTS OF JUSTICE ACT
, R.S.Q., c. T-16:

21.
The Superior
Court, which is a court of record, is composed of 144 judges including a Chief
Justice, a Senior Associate Chief Justice and an Associate Chief Justice.

[…]

[
17
]

CODE OF CIVIL
PROCEDURE
(C.C.P.),
R.S.Q., c. C-25:

46.
The courts and judges have all the powers necessary for the
exercise of their jurisdiction.

They may, at any time and in all
matters, whether in first instance or in appeal, issue orders to safeguard the
rights of the parties, for such time and on such conditions as they may
determine. As well, they may, in the matters brought before them, even on their
own initiative, issue injunctions or reprimands, suppress writings or declare
them libellous, and make such orders as are appropriate to deal with cases for
which no specific remedy is provided by law.

[
18
]

RULES OF
PRACTICE OF THE SUPERIOR COURT OF QUEBEC IN CIVIL MATTERS
(R.C.P. (S.C.))
R.R.Q., 1981, c.
C-25, r. 8
:

CHAPTER XV – QUARRELSOME CONDUCT

84.

If a person acts in a quarrelsome manner, that is if that person exercises
litigious rights in an excessive or unreasonable manner, the Court may prohibit
that person from instituting an action or an application without having first
obtained prior judicial authorization.

85.

The order of prohibition is general or is limited to one or more judicial
districts, or with respect to one or more persons. In an extreme case, the
order of prohibition may include an order preventing the person from having
access to the courthouse.

86.

The application to institute or to continue an action or application is
presented to the Chief Justice or the judge designated by the Chief Justice,
and is filed in the Office of the Court for the District of Quebec or the
District of Montreal depending on the division in which the order of
prohibition was issued.
[3]
The application may be adjudicated on the basis of the record,
without a hearing.

87.

The application to institute an action must be accompanied by the order of
prohibition and the proceeding the applicant seeks to institute.

88.

The Chief Justice or the judge designated by the Chief Justice may refer the
application to institute an action to the Court, in which case the applicant
must serve it on the parties contemplated by the proposed proceeding, with a
ten-day notice of presentation.

89.

An unauthorized proceeding is deemed never to have existed. When informed of an
order of prohibition, the Clerk must refuse the acceptance of an unauthorized
proceeding, except for an application to institute or continue proceedings or
an inscription in appeal.

90.

The Clerk shall transmit a copy of an order of prohibition filed at the Office
of the Clerk to the Clerks of all the judicial districts and to the Chief
Justice in Montreal for inclusion in the public registry of persons subject to
orders of prohibition

ANALYSIS

I.
Preliminary
comments
:

[
19
]

Access to an independent tribunal is a
fundamental right (
s. 23
of the
Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms
,
R.S.Q., c. C-12).  As a general rule, a citizen can file a claim on his or her
behalf at any time without prior authorization of a judge or of the opposing
party.

[
20
]

Occasionally, a citizen may clearly abuse the
right to file a claim or other proceedings before a court or other tribunal.
In such exceptional cases, an aggrieved party may seek an order restricting the
ability of the vexatious litigant to initiate proceedings or to continue
previously instituted proceedings.  Morin J., as he then was, wrote in
Gignac

c.
Girard
, (S.C. Bonaventure, file no. 105-05-000059-952, judgment
of July 10, 1996):

Si l’accès aux tribunaux est un
principe sacré dans notre société, il s’agit d’un droit dont, comme tout autre
droit, il ne faut pas abuser.  Or, le demandeur a clairement abusé de son droit
d’ester en justice et il y a lieu, en conséquence, de baliser désormais ce
droit, dans le cas du demandeur, de sorte qu’il l’utilise à bon escient.

[
21
]

In other words, a court, or at least a superior
court, has the inherent power to ensure that its process is not abused by
proceedings without any apparent reasonable ground, so as to be vexatious and
harassing (
Metropolitan Bank Ltd
v.
Pooley
, (1884-85) 10 App. Cases 210;
Droit de la famille
– 2500,
J.E. 96-1846 (C.A.)
;
Yorke

c.
Paskell-Mede
,
1996 CanLII 4513 (QC CS)
, [1996] R.J.Q. 1964 (S.C.);
Droit de la famille
–
92,
[1983] C.S. 1138
).  In any case,
article 46

C.C.P.

confers such power on all the courts of Quebec governed by its provisions, and
section 40 of the
Federal Courts Act
, R.S.C., c. F-7 specifically
empowers the Federal Court and the Federal Court of Appeal to declare a
litigant to be vexatious.

[
22
]

For other courts or tribunals which are not so
empowered, the Superior Court may enjoin a vexatious litigant from introducing
proceedings and order the proper official to refuse to receive such proceedings
without some prior authorization.  In such case, one can speak of an injunctive
remedy (see for example:
Barreau du Québec
c.
Ethier
, B.E. 2003
B.E.-407 (S.C.)).

[
23
]

The order may be restricted to proceedings in a
file or against a particular defendant, which is usually the case.  Sometime,
it restricts access to the court in general.  Article 85
R.P.C. (S.C.)

recognises that distinction.  The prohibition order, when issued by the
Superior Court, may even be broader, restricting access to all courts and
tribunals (I doubt however that the Superior Court may restrict access to a
higher court such as the Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court of Canada, or to
a federal court).

[
24
]

Finally, it is appropriate to bear in mind three
other points.  First, the Superior Court is a court of record (
Courts of
Justice

Act
, s. 21).  This means that every legal proceeding filed
with it must be properly recorded, archived and accessible to the public.
[4]

This principle must apply to any application for authorization to file a
proceeding and to the response of the judge who deals with it; this is
especially true in case of a refusal that may amount to a summary dismissal of
the proposed claim.  Second, the request for authorization should be made in a
manner that is compatible with the
Code of Civil Procedure
, that is, by
way of a motion (
articles 564

C.C.P
.), supported by an affidavit
(
art. 88

C.C.P.
), outlining the reasons why authorization is being
sought, addressed to the Chief Justice (article 86
R.P.C. (S.C.)
),
including the prohibition order and the proposed proceedings (article 87
R.P.C.
(S.C.)
) and filed in the office of the Court where the prohibition order
was issued (article 86
R.P.C. (S.C.)
, French version)
[5]

(
S.M.B.D.- Jewish Hospital
v.
Saraffian
,
[2004] J.Q. no. 12149,
par. 26
, 27 and 28 (C.A.)).  To proceed in this fashion is not only in
accordance with the
Code of

Civil Procedure
, but it is also the
sole means for the petitioner to interrupt the applicable prescriptive period
(article 2892
C.C.Q
.), a benefit that cannot be derived from a mere
letter sent by fax or otherwise to the Chief Justice.  Thirdly, since the Clerk
of the Court may open no new file without the prior authorization of the Chief
Justice, the said motion must bear the number of the file in which the
prohibition order was issued (in this case, no. 455-05-000418-009).

II.
Legal
status of the Chief Justice’s reply
:

[
25
]

Upon a review of the motion, including the
affidavit, the prohibition order, the proposed proceedings and the exhibits
that a petitioner may wish to add, the Chief Justice may conclude that the
intended proceeding is
prima facie
one more example of an excessive or
unreasonable exercise of a litigious right by the petitioner, and he may then
decide the authorization,
ex parte
, as provided for in article
86
R.P.C. (S.C)
.  If the situation is not clear, it may be wise to hold a hearing,
where the targeted defendant would be provided an opportunity to contest the
application for authorization, as provided for in article 88
R.P.C. (S.C.)
.

[
26
]

In this case, Rolland, C.J. decided to deny
authorization without a hearing and any notice to the potential defendants.

[
27
]

In my opinion, such a response constituted a
judgment, rendered after the application was taken under advisement.  It
therefore had to be recorded, and the sole obvious place was the file in which
the prohibition order was issued.

[
28
]

Considering the consequences of a refusal on the
potential rights of a petitioner, including the extinction of his/her claim for
damages, it has to be reasoned, even when
article 471

C.C.P.
does
not apply because it was decided
ex parte
; this obligation flows from
the rules of natural justice (
Baker
v.
Canada (Minister of
Citizenship and Immigration
,
1999 CanLII 699 (SCC)
, [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817;
R.
v.
Sheppard
,

2002 SCC 26 (CanLII)
, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 869).

III.
The proper
way to appeal
:

[
29
]

Relying on the judgment of LeBel, J.A., as he
was then, in
Morency
c.
Commission des affaires sociales
,
1998 CanLII 12681 (QC CA)
, J.E.
98-703 (C.A.), Astral and Pixcom submit that  leave to appeal was necessary.
Mr. Fabrikant responds that no such authorization was required since the
decision of Rolland, C.J. amounts to a final judgment disposing of his claims
that total close to one million dollars.

[
30
]

It is obvious that Mr.  Fabrikant sought
authorization to file a claim against Astral and Pixcom because of the
prohibition order.  In other words, his request was made pursuant to the
judgment of May 30, 2000.  For the reasons outlined by LeBel, J.A. in
Morency
,
I am of the view that such judgment can be appealed
only
with leave:

Le juge en chef associé de la Cour
supérieure a été saisi de la demande de monsieur Morency en raison d’un
jugement antérieur de la Cour supérieure, rendu par le juge Jean Richard, le 17
février 1996.  Sur requête de la C.S.S.T., celui-ci avait interdit à l’appelant
de présenter toute nouvelle procédure relative à son accident du travail devant
la Cour supérieure, sans autorisation d’un de ses juges (dossier no.
200-05-002931-934).  La procédure soumise au juge en chef associé de la Cour
supérieure a donc été présentée en exécution de ce jugement.

Pour ce motif, tout pourvoi
contre cette décision est assujetti à l’autorisation préalable d’un juge de
notre Cour, suivant l’
article 26

C.p.c.
Il s’assimile à un jugement en matière
d’exécution, au sens du sous-alinéa 3 du dernier paragraphe de l’article 26
C.p.c.
Sous l’article 26, l’autorisation de
pourvoi exige non seulement de constater que le jugement soit susceptible
d’appel, mais suppose une évaluation de la valeur de l’appel proposé et de ses
conséquences pour la saine administration de la justice.

(je souligne)

[
31
]

This view is consistent with the broad
interpretation generally given to sub-par. 3 of par. 2
of art. 26 C.P.C. (
Québec (Ministre de la Santé et des Services sociaux

c.
Association des chirurgiens dentistes du Québec
,
J.E. 2002-703
(C.A.)
;
Droit de la famille-2453
,
1996 CanLII 5713 (QC CA)
, J.E. 96-1434 (C.A., Marie Deschamps,
J.A, as she was then, single judge);
Boutin
c.
Dubois
,
[2003]
J.Q. no 9503
(C.A., Jacques Chamberland, J.A., single judge)).

[
32
]

Failure to have obtained leave to appeal goes to
the heart of the jurisdiction of the Court and is fatal here (
Selig
c.
Chrétien
,

1994 CanLII 5652 (QC CA)
, [1994] R.D.J. 323 (C.A.);
2847-3858 Quebec inc.
c.
Phabz Investments
Inc.
,
J.E. 94-1543 (C.A.)
) since leave pursuant to
article 523

C.C.P.

was not sought.  In any case, if such leave had been sought, I would have
refused it for the reasons outlined below.

IV.
The
status of Pixcom and Astral
:

[
33
]

Once Robert, C.J.Q. had ordered that the
inscription in appeal be served on Astral and Pixcom
[6]
, they were entitled
to contest Mr. Fabrikant's appeal.  They became parties to the appeal, in
a way similar to what is prescribed by article 88
R.P.C. (S.C.)
when the
application to institute an action is deferred by the Chief Justice to a judge
of the Superior Court.  Therefore, they could make a motion to dismiss the
appeal.

V.
Comments
on the claim of Mr. Fabrikant
:

[
34
]

Although, strictly speaking, it is not necessary
to dispose of the motions to dismiss the appeal since the appeal was
irregularly filed, I would add that it seems obvious to me that once a litigant
has been declared vexatious, the allegations of any new proceedings that he/she
is making and for which an authorization must be sought cannot be presumed not
to be vexatious.  Therefore, such an applicant has the burden to establish
prima
facie
the seriousness of the claim for which he/she is seeking
authorization
[7]
.

[
35
]

The application of Mr. Fabrikant made to
the Chief Justice of the Superior Court consisted only of the draft statement
of claim I have quoted at length in paragraph [12] above.  Based on its
content, I am of the view that Mr. Fabrikant did not discharge the burden incumbent
on him to establish
prima facie
to Rolland, C.J. that his new claim was
no more than another example of his predisposition to abuse the legal system.

[
36
]

In other words, the proposed statement of claim
did not refute the presumption that Mr. Fabrikant was trying, once more,
to abuse the legal system.  On the contrary, paragraph 4 of his draft statement
of claim shows that he still denies that he committed the most serious offence,
murder; instead, he refers once more to his thesis that he was provoked and
forced to use violence because of various plots against him.  This thesis, that
he would have to prove in order to establish that Pixcom and Astral made
malicious comments about him, has been consistently rejected by the courts, and
to give him yet another opportunity to argue it would be nothing more than a
flagrant abuse of the legal system.  Chief Justice Rolland’s response was
succinct but well founded: Mr. Fabrikant had not shown a serious cause of
action against Pixcom and Astral in his application for authorization.

CONCLUSION

[
37
]

Accordingly, I would grant the motions to
dismiss the appeal, with costs, and dismiss the appeal, with costs.

PIERRE J.
DALPHOND, J.A.

[1]
The Federal Court declared Mr. Fabrikant a vexatious litigant
on November 1, 1999 (file T-376-99).

[2]
During the hearing, the Court said that it would not adjudicate
this last conclusion.

[3]
The French version reads:

La
demande d’autorisation est adressée au juge en chef ou au juge désigné par lui
et
déposée au greffe d’où origine l’ordonnance
[…]

[4]
In
Dixon
v
. Mackay
(1902) 21 Man. R.762 reference
is made to
Stephen’s Commentaries
, vol. 3, p. 272, where a Court of
Record is defined as:

“ One whereof the acts and
judicial proceedings are enrolled for a perpetual memorial and testimony; which
rolls are called the records of the Court, and are of such high and super
eminent authority that their truth is not to be called in question.”

Also:
Rex
v.
Porhorliuk
,
(1918)
1918 CanLII 370 (AB SCAD)
, 30 C.C.C. 281.

[5]
The French version should prevail as it more accurately
reflects how the process actually works, or should work.

[6]
The motion to obtain leave to appeal from a judgment refusing
ex
parte
an authorization to file a statement of claim does not have to be
served on the potential defendants since they are not parties.  However the
motion judge may order, if he/she thinks it necessary or useful, that it be
served on them.

[7]
If the authorization is granted, the ordinary rules of the
Code
of civil Procedure
will apply to the new proceedings.
